mcqs: At resonance X_L = X_C, so the impedance is purely resistive (Z = R).
Current and voltage are in phase: phase difference 0.
A sine wave is the natural output of a rotating-coil generator and is the only waveform whose shape is unchanged by inductors, capacitors and transformers.
It produces the least disturbance (distortion, harmonics, interference) in electrical circuits.
V = V₀ sin ωt with ω = 157 rad s⁻¹.
X_L = 2πfL, so inductive reactance increases in proportion to frequency (R does not depend on frequency).
An alternating quantity v = V₀ sin(ωt + φ) is completely known when its maximum value V₀, its frequency and its phase φ are known.
Maxwell added the displacement current ε₀ dΦ_E/dt to Ampere's law: ∮B·dl = μ₀(I + ε₀ dΦ_E/dt).
This generalised Ampere's law led to the prediction of electromagnetic waves.

s: When an electromagnetic wave passes from air into glass its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency does not change.
Of the choices, radio waves, X-rays and ultraviolet are all electromagnetic waves; ultrasound is a mechanical (sound) wave, not electromagnetic.
mcqs.n: The printed choices do not match the stem (they list radiations, not quantities). The quantity that does not change is the frequency; read as 'which is not an electromagnetic wave', the answer is D (ultrasound).

s: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) with X_L = 2πfL rising and X_C = 1/(2πfC) falling as f increases.
Below the resonant frequency Z decreases as f rises; at resonance Z = R (minimum); above resonance Z increases.
So the impedance neither always increases nor always decreases; X_C decreases while X_L increases.
mcqs.n: No single printed choice is correct for every frequency (the label (D) is also printed twice). Above resonance the impedance increases (B); below resonance it decreases (C).

shortQuestions: ε = −L ΔI/Δt, so a graph of induced e.m.f. against rate of change of current is a straight line through the origin (with negative slope, since the e.m.f. opposes the change).
The magnitude of the gradient equals the self-inductance L of the coil.
For a resistor the current and voltage are in phase: they change sign together.
Instantaneous power p = vi = V₀I₀ sin²ωt is the product of two quantities of the same sign, so it is always positive (or zero).
Energy always flows from the generator into the resistor; average power = V_rmsI_rms.
X_L = 2πfL, so a graph of X_L against f is a straight line through the origin.
Its gradient is 2πL, determined by the inductance L of the coil.
(a) X_L = 2πfL ∝ f: doubling the frequency doubles the inductive reactance.
(b) X_C = 1/(2πfC) ∝ 1/f: doubling the frequency halves the capacitive reactance.
Inductor: X_L = ωL. Unit: s⁻¹ × H = s⁻¹ × V s A⁻¹ = V A⁻¹ = Ω.
Capacitor: X_C = 1/(ωC). Unit: 1/(s⁻¹ × F) = 1/(s⁻¹ × C V⁻¹) = V s C⁻¹ = V A⁻¹ = Ω.
So both reactances are measured in ohms.
The heart muscle produces small electrical potentials as it contracts and relaxes (depolarisation and repolarisation of its cells).
These potential differences (about 1 mV) spread through the body and are picked up by electrodes placed on the skin.
An electrocardiograph amplifies and records them against time; the trace (P wave, QRS complex, T wave) shows the heart's rhythm and helps diagnose heart disease.
longQuestions: For i = I₀ sin ωt: the peak value I₀ is the maximum value in a cycle; the mean value over a full cycle is zero, and over a half cycle I_mean = 2I₀/π = 0.637 I₀.
The r.m.s. (effective) value is the steady d.c. current that would produce the same heating in a resistor: I_rms = √(mean of i²).
i² = I₀² sin²ωt = I₀²(1 − cos 2ωt)/2. Over a cycle the mean of cos 2ωt is zero, so mean of i² = I₀²/2.
I_rms = I₀/√2 = 0.707 I₀. Similarly V_rms = V₀/√2 and V_mean (half cycle) = 2V₀/π.
Instantaneous voltage: v = V₀ sin ωt.
By Ohm's law the instantaneous current is i = v/R = (V₀/R) sin ωt = I₀ sin ωt; current is in phase with voltage (φ = 0).
Instantaneous power p = vi = V₀I₀ sin²ωt, always positive.
Average power per cycle: P = V₀I₀ × mean(sin²ωt) = V₀I₀/2 = V_rmsI_rms = I_rms²R. The phasors V and I point in the same direction.
Instantaneous voltage: v = V₀ sin ωt; charge on the capacitor q = Cv = CV₀ sin ωt.
Current i = dq/dt = ωCV₀ cos ωt = I₀ sin(ωt + π/2), with I₀ = V₀/X_C and X_C = 1/(ωC). The current leads the voltage by 90°.
Instantaneous power p = vi = V₀I₀ sin ωt cos ωt = ½V₀I₀ sin 2ωt, which is positive for one quarter cycle (capacitor charging) and negative for the next (returning energy).
Average power per cycle = 0: a pure capacitor dissipates no energy.
Impedance Z is the total opposition of an a.c. circuit to current, combining resistance and reactance: Z = V_rms/I_rms, measured in ohms.
In a series RLC circuit the same current I flows through all; V_R = IR is in phase with I, V_L = IX_L leads I by 90°, V_C = IX_C lags I by 90°.
From the phasor diagram: V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = I√(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).
Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²), with phase angle tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.
At resonance X_L = X_C, Z = R (minimum) and f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
A source of e.m.f. ε with internal resistance r supplies a load R: I = ε/(R + r), and the power in the load is P = I²R = ε²R/(R + r)².
For maximum P, dP/dR = 0: ε²[(R + r)² − 2R(R + r)]/(R + r)⁴ = 0, which gives R = r.
So maximum power is delivered when the load resistance equals the internal resistance; then P_max = ε²/(4r) (efficiency 50%).

For a.c. circuits the same result holds with impedances: maximum power is transferred when the load impedance matches the source impedance (conjugate match, e.g. a transformer used to match a loudspeaker to an amplifier).
In a series RL circuit the current lags the applied voltage.
Take the current I as reference phasor. V_R = IR is in phase with I; V_L = IX_L leads I by 90°.
The applied voltage V is the phasor sum: V = √(V_R² + V_L²) = I√(R² + X_L²), so Z = √(R² + X_L²).
V is ahead of I by angle φ with tan φ = X_L/R = ωL/R. Thus the current lags the voltage by φ (0 < φ < 90°).
In a series RC circuit the current leads the applied voltage.
Take the current I as reference. V_R = IR is in phase with I; V_C = IX_C lags I by 90°.
Phasor sum: V = √(V_R² + V_C²) = I√(R² + X_C²), so Z = √(R² + X_C²).
V is behind I by angle φ with tan φ = X_C/R = 1/(ωCR). So the current leads the voltage by φ (0 < φ < 90°).

Maxwell's equations: (1) Gauss's law for electricity: ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀. (2) Gauss's law for magnetism: ∮B·dA = 0 (no isolated poles). (3) Faraday's law: ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt. (4) Ampere–Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = μ₀(I + ε₀ dΦ_E/dt).

Induced electric field: a changing magnetic flux through a circular path of radius r induces an e.m.f. ε = ΔΦ/Δt round it. Since ε = ∮E·dl = E(2πr), E = (1/2πr)(ΔΦ/Δt). With Φ = AB, E = (A/2πr)(ΔB/Δt).

Displacement current: between capacitor plates no charge flows, but the electric flux Φ_E = EA = q/ε₀ changes. Then Δq/Δt = ε₀ ΔΦ_E/Δt, so the displacement current is I_d = ε₀ ΔΦ_E/Δt, which completes the circuit for Ampere's law.
Together these show that changing E and B fields generate each other, giving electromagnetic waves moving at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).
A metal detector uses electromagnetic induction. A transmitter coil carries an alternating (or pulsed) current and produces a changing magnetic field.
When a metal object comes into this field, eddy currents are induced in it; these produce their own magnetic field.
This secondary field induces a small voltage in a receiver coil (or changes the inductance/frequency of the search coil).
The electronic circuit detects the change and gives a sound or signal. Used at airports, for security checks, and to locate buried pipes, mines and coins.
